newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk Islamists say no U-turn despite army.
newsitem.headline: Turk Islamists say no U-turn despite army.

text.p: Turkey's ruling Islamists said on Friday they had not given up their mission to increase the role of religion in public life despite giving in to army demands for a crackdown on Islamic activism.
"There has been no turnaround in our assessments," Islam-based Welfare Party deputy Salih Kapusuz told a news conference.
The cabinet agreed on Thursday to fully enforce a list of army demands against rising Islamist fervour that the military says is endangering NATO member Turkey's official secularism.
Turkish newspapers quoted Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, the Welfare leader, as making an unfamiliar call to ministers to beware of religious extremism.

"We are also against fundamentalism. Fundamentalism means backwardness. It has nothing to do with Islam," the Sabah newspaper quoted Erbakan as saying at the cabinet gathering. Leaks from government meetings often appear in the press.

The unity of Erbakan's coalition with the secularist True Path Party had been under strain for the past two weeks while he stalled on gaining cabinet approval for the army measures, which hit at the heart of his constituency.
Erbakan came to power in coalition last June partly on a promise to revive the status of Islam in Turkey.
But recent proposals for mild Islamist reforms angered the generals, who demanded full implementation of secularist laws dating to the 1920s.
The army, which has staged three coups in the last 37 years, also wants Erbakan to pass new legislation to crack down on peaceful Islamist dissent.

The military last year forced Erbakan to backtrack on previous promises to scrap a military accord with Israel and throw out a Western air force that patrols north Iraq from a base in southern Turkey.
Ministers have said they would implement the anti-Islamist clamp down in three phases, suggesting the prime minister may try to play for time.
But the secularist Hurriyet daily said that even an insincere committment by Erbakan to an anti-Islamist programme was meaningful.

"It was the first time Erbakan has talked about the struggle against fundamentalism," the paper quoted an unnamed minister from the True Path wing as saying. "Even if he is not sincere, it is an important development," the minister said.
The Islamists are due to hand over power to True Path leader Tansu Ciller, the foreign minister, next year under a powersharing deal.
But commentators say Erbakan is likely to break the coalition before then and go for early polls in the hope of gaining a majority in parliament that would allow him to carry out his Islamist agenda.
"I don't know anyone who believes he will hand over to Ciller," a Western diplomat said.
